text: Gallium is a chemical element with the symbol Ga and atomic number 31. It was discovered by the French chemist Paul-Émile Lecoq de Boisbaudran in Paris, France, in 1875. Elemental gallium is a soft, silvery metal at standard temperature and pressure, and in its liquid state, it appears silvery white. When sufficient force is applied, solid gallium fractures conchoidally. Its melting point is 29.7646 °C (85.5763 °F; 302.9146 K), which is just above room temperature and approximately equal to average summer daytime temperatures in Earth's mid-latitudes. This melting point is used as a temperature reference point in the International Temperature Scale of 1990 (ITS-90) established by the International Bureau of Weights and Measures (BIPM), and the triple point of gallium, 302.9166 K (29.7666 °C, 85.5799 °F), is preferred by the US National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST). Gallium melts in a person's hands at normal human body temperature of 37.0 °C (98.6 °F) and has a strong tendency to supercool below its melting point; Ga nanoparticles can remain liquid below 90 K, and seeding with a crystal helps initiate freezing. Gallium is one of four non-radioactive metals (with caesium, rubidium, and mercury) that are liquid at or near room temperature; unlike mercury, it is neither highly reactive nor highly toxic and can be used in metal-in-glass high-temperature thermometers. It has one of the largest liquid ranges for a metal and a low vapor pressure at high temperatures. Its boiling point is 2676 K, nearly nine times higher than its melting point on the absolute scale, the greatest ratio between melting point and boiling point of any element. Liquid gallium wets glass and skin, as well as most other materials (except quartz, graphite, gallium(III) oxide, and PTFE), making it mechanically difficult to handle. Gallium's volume expands by 3.10% when it changes from liquid to solid, requiring care when storing it in containers that may rupture. It shares the higher-density liquid state with water, silicon, germanium, bismuth, and plutonium. Gallium does not occur as a free element in nature but is found in trace amounts as gallium(III) compounds in zinc ores like sphalerite and in bauxite. It is obtained by smelting and is a silvery blue metal that fractures conchoidally like glass. Gallium does not crystallize in simple crystal structures; its stable phase under normal conditions is orthorhombic with 8 atoms per conventional unit cell, where each atom has one nearest neighbor at 244 pm, and the remaining six neighbors are spaced at 27, 30, and 39 pm, grouped in pairs. The bonding between nearest neighbors is covalent, forming Ga₂ dimers, which explains its low melting point compared to aluminum and indium. This structure is similar to iodine and results from interactions between gallium's single 4p electrons, farther from the nucleus than the 4s electrons and the [Ar]3d¹⁰ core. In the liquid state, gallium exhibits a complex low-coordinated structure where each atom is surrounded by 10 others, rather than the 11–12 typical of most liquid metals. The physical properties of gallium are highly anisotropic, with significant differences between linear and volume thermal expansion coefficients, especially near the melting point, where the coefficient of thermal expansion increases by several hundred percent upon melting. Gallium has 30 known isotopes, ranging from mass number 60 to 89; only two are stable and occur naturally: gallium-69 (60.1% abundance) and gallium-71 (39.9% abundance). All other isotopes are radioactive; gallium-67 has the longest half-life at 3.2617 days. Isotopes lighter than gallium-69 decay via beta plus decay or electron capture to zinc isotopes, while those heavier than gallium-71 decay via beta minus decay to germanium isotopes; gallium-70 can decay to either zinc-70 or germanium-70. Gallium-67 and gallium-68 (half-life 67.84 minutes) are used in nuclear medicine imaging. Gallium primarily exists in the +3 oxidation state, with the +1 state found in some compounds, such as GaCl₂, which contains both gallium(I) and gallium(III) and can be formulated as GaIGaIIICl₄; the monochloride is unstable above 0 °C and disproportionates into elemental gallium and gallium(III) chloride. True gallium(II) compounds include GaS (formulated as Ga₂⁴⁺(S²⁻)₂) and Ga₂Cl₄(C₄H₈O₂)₂. Strong acids dissolve gallium, forming gallium(III) salts such as Ga(NO₃)₃, and aqueous solutions contain the hydrated ion [Ga(H₂O)₆]³⁺. Gallium(III) hydroxide, Ga(OH)₃, can be precipitated from gallium(III) solutions by adding ammonia and dehydrated at 100 °C to form gallium oxide hydroxide, GaO(OH). Alkaline hydroxide solutions dissolve gallium, forming gallate salts containing the Ga(OH)₄⁻ anion; gallium hydroxide, which is amphoteric, also dissolves in alkali to form gallate salts. Gallium reacts with chalcogens at high temperatures; at room temperature, it is unreactive with air and water due to a protective oxide layer, but at higher temperatures, it reacts with oxygen to form gallium(III) oxide, Ga₂O₃. Reducing Ga₂O₃ with elemental gallium at 500–700 °C yields dark brown gallium(I) oxide, Ga₂O, a strong reducing agent capable of reducing H₂SO₄ to H₂S, which disproportionates back to gallium and Ga₂O₃ at 800 °C. Gallium(III) sulfide, Ga₂S₃, has three crystal modifications and can be formed by reacting gallium with H₂S at 950 °C or Ga(OH)₃ at 747 °C. Reacting alkali metal carbonates and Ga₂O₃ with H₂S produces thiogallates containing the [Ga₂S₄]²⁻ anion, which decompose in strong acids to release H₂S; HgGa₂S₄ is used as a phosphor. Gallium also forms lower oxidation state sulfides, such as gallium(II) sulfide and green gallium(I) sulfide, produced by heating gallium(II) sulfide to 1000 °C under nitrogen. The binary chalcogenides Ga₂Se₃ and Ga₂Te₃ have the zincblende structure and are semiconductors but are easily hydrolyzed and have limited utility. Gallium reacts with ammonia at 1050 °C to form gallium nitride (GaN), and forms binary compounds with phosphorus, arsenic, and antimony: gallium phosphide (GaP), gallium arsenide (GaAs), and gallium antimonide (GaSb), all with the same structure as ZnS and important semiconducting properties. These compounds are synthesized by direct reaction of gallium with elemental phosphorus, arsenic, or antimony, or by reacting Ga₂O with phosphorus at low temperatures; GaP also exhibits higher electrical conductivity than GaN. Gallium forms ternary nitrides, such as examples with lithium and phosphorus or arsenic (e.g., Li₃GaP₂ and Li₃GaAs₂), which are easily hydrolyzed by dilute acids and water. Gallium(III) oxide reacts with fluorinating agents like HF or F₂ to form gallium(III) fluoride, GaF₃, an ionic compound insoluble in water but soluble in hydrofluoric acid, forming GaF₃·3H₂O; dehydration of this adduct forms GaF₂OH·nH₂O, and the adduct reacts with ammonia to form GaF₃·3NH₃, which can be heated to form anhydrous GaF₃. Gallium trichloride is formed by reacting gallium metal with chlorine gas and exists as dimeric molecules, Ga₂Cl₆, with a melting point of 78 °C; similar dimers exist with bromine and iodine. Like other group 13 trihalides, gallium(III) halides are Lewis acids, reacting with alkali metal halides to form salts with GaX⁻₄ anions and with alkyl halides to form carbocations and GaX⁻₄. When heated, gallium(III) halides react with elemental gallium to form gallium(I) halides; for example, GaCl₃ reacts with Ga to form GaCl. At lower temperatures, the equilibrium shifts back, and GaCl disproportionates into elemental gallium and GaCl₃. GaCl can also be produced by reacting gallium with HCl at 950 °C, yielding a red solid. Gallium(I) compounds are stabilized by forming adducts with Lewis acids; so-called "gallium(II) halides," GaX₂, are actually adducts with the structure Ga⁺[GaX₄]⁻. Gallium forms a hydride, GaH₃ (gallane), produced by reacting lithium gallium hydride (LiGaH₄) with gallium(III) chloride at −30 °C. In the presence of dimethyl ether, gallane polymerizes to (GaH₃)ₙ; without solvent, it forms dimer Ga₂H₆ (digallane), a gas with a structure similar to diborane, unlike α-AlH₃ where aluminum has a coordination number of 6. Gallane is unstable above −10 °C and decomposes into elemental gallium and hydrogen. Organogallium compounds are less reactive than organoaluminum compounds but more reactive than organothallium compounds; alkylgalliums are monomeric, and Lewis acidity decreases in the order Al > Ga > In, so organogallium compounds do not form bridged dimers. They form stable peroxides and are liquids at room temperature with low melting points, being mobile and flammable. Triphenylgallium is monomeric in solution but forms chain structures in crystals due to weak Ga···C interactions. Gallium trichloride is a common starting reagent for organogallium compound synthesis, such as in carbogallation reactions, and reacts with lithium cyclopentadienide in diethyl ether to form the trigonal planar gallium cyclopentadienyl complex GaC.

Organoindium compounds are less reactive than organoaluminium compounds but more reactive than organothallium compounds. Alkylgallium compounds are monomeric, and Lewis acidity decreases in the order Al > Ga > In, meaning organogallium compounds do not form bridged dimers like organoaluminium compounds. Organogallium compounds are less reactive than organoaluminium compounds and do form stable peroxides. These alkylgalliums are liquids at room temperature with low melting points, are mobile, and are flammable. Triphenylgallium is monomeric in solution but forms chain structures in crystals due to weak Ga···C interactions. Gallium trichloride is a common starting reagent for forming organogallium compounds, such as in carbogallation reactions; it reacts with lithium cyclopentadienide in diethyl ether to form the trigonal planar gallium cyclopentadienyl complex GaCp3. Gallium(I) forms complexes with arene ligands like hexamethylbenzene, which is bulky enough to give a half-sandwich structure [Ga(η6-C6Me6)]+, while less bulky ligands such as mesitylene allow two ligands to bind in a bent sandwich structure. Benzene, being even less bulky, allows dimer formation, as in [Ga(η6-C6H6)2][GaCl4]·3C6H6. In 1871, Dmitri Mendeleev predicted the existence of gallium, naming it "eka-aluminium" and accurately forecasting its density, melting point, oxide character, and bonding in chloride. He predicted eka-aluminium would be discovered by spectroscope, would dissolve slowly in acids and alkalis, not react with air, that M2O3 would dissolve in acids to form MX3 salts, that eka-aluminium salts would form basic salts, that eka-aluminium sulfate would form alums, and that anhydrous MCl3 would be more volatile than ZnCl2—all of which were later confirmed. Gallium was discovered in 1875 by French chemist Paul-Émile Lecoq de Boisbaudran using spectroscopy from a sample of sphalerite, and he later obtained the free metal by electrolysis of its hydroxide in potassium hydroxide solution. He named the element "gallia" from Latin Gallia, meaning Gaul, his native region, and it was later speculated (though denied by Lecoq in 1877) that he named it after himself due to "le coq" (rooster) and "gallus" (rooster). De Boisbaudran initially measured gallium's density as 4.7 g/cm³, which did not match Mendeleev's prediction; Mendeleev suggested a remeasurement, which yielded the correct value of 5.9 g/cm³, exactly as predicted. From 1875 until the semiconductor era, gallium's primary uses were high-temperature thermometry and metal alloys with unusual stability or low melting points, some of which are liquid at room temperature. The development of gallium arsenide as a direct bandgap semiconductor in the 1960s marked the most significant stage in gallium's applications. In the late 1960s, the electronics industry began using gallium commercially for light-emitting diodes, photovoltaics, and semiconductors, while the metals industry used it to reduce alloy melting points. First blue gallium nitride LEDs were developed in 1971–1973 but were weak; only in the early 1990s did Shuji Nakamura combine GaN with indium gallium nitride to develop modern blue LEDs, now the basis of ubiquitous white LEDs, commercialized by Nichia in 1993. Nakamura and two other Japanese scientists received a Nobel Prize in Physics in 2014 for this work. Global gallium production slowly increased from several tens of tons per year in the 1970s to about 100 t/yr by 2010 and rapidly accelerated, reaching approximately 450 t/yr by 2024. Gallium does not exist as a free element in Earth's crust; high-content minerals like gallite (CuGaS2) are too rare to serve as primary sources. Its crustal abundance is approximately 16.9 ppm, making it the 34th most abundant element, comparable to lead, cobalt, and niobium. Unlike these elements, gallium does not form its own ore deposits with concentrations above 0.1 wt.% and occurs at trace levels in zinc ores (~50 ppm) and slightly higher in aluminum ores, extracted as a by-product. This lack of enrichment is due to gallium's geochemical behavior. The USGS estimates over 1 million tons of gallium is contained in known bauxite and zinc ore reserves. Some coal flue dusts contain small amounts of gallium, typically less than 1% by weight, but these are not extractable without mining the host materials. Gallium is produced exclusively as a by-product during processing of bauxite and sulfidic zinc ores (mainly sphalerite), with minor amounts from coal. During the Bayer process, gallium accumulates in sodium hydroxide liquor and is extracted via methods such as ion-exchange resins; at a typical feed concentration of 50 ppm, about 15% of the gallium is extractable. The remainder goes to red mud and aluminum hydroxide streams. Gallium is removed from the resin in solution and then electrolyzed to produce gallium metal. For semiconductor use, it is further purified by zone melting or the Czochralski process, achieving purities of 99.9999% routinely and commercially. Gallium production is constrained by the annual extraction of bauxite, sulfidic zinc ores, and coal. Supply potential is defined as economically extractable amounts under current market conditions and includes at least 2,100 t/yr from bauxite, 85 t/yr from sulfidic zinc ores, and potentially 590 t/yr from coal—significantly exceeding current production of 375 t in 2016. The average price for low-grade gallium was $120 per kg in 2016 and $135–140 per kg in 2017. In 2017, world low-grade gallium production was about 315 tons, a 15% decrease from 2016. China, Japan, South Korea, Russia, and Ukraine were leading producers, while Germany ceased primary production in 2016. High-purity gallium production was about 180 tons in 2017, mostly from China, Japan, Slovakia, the UK, and the U.S. The 2017 annual production capacity was estimated at 730 tons for low-grade and 320 tons for refined gallium. China produced about 250 tons of low-grade gallium in 2016 and 300 tons in 2017, accounting for more than half of global LED production. As of July 2023, China produced between 80% and 95% of global gallium output. As of August 2023, China produced 80% of the world's gallium and 60% of germanium, and began restricting exports of both, key materials in the semiconductor industry, amid a "chip war" with the U.S. In 2024, China produced 98% of the world’s low-purity gallium (USGS). Semiconductor applications dominate commercial demand, accounting for 98% of total use, with 44% used in light fixtures and 36% in integrated circuits, and smaller shares in photovoltaics and magnets. Extremely high-purity gallium (>99.9999%) is commercially available for semiconductors. In 2007, gallium arsenide and gallium nitride in electronic components accounted for about 98% of U.S. gallium consumption, with 66% used in integrated circuits (mostly GaAs) for ultra-high-speed logic chips and MESFETs in cell phones, and 20% in optoelectronics. Worldwide, gallium arsenide makes up 95% of annual gallium consumption, valued at $7.5 billion in 2016, with 53% from cell phones, 27% from wireless communications, and the rest from automotive, consumer, fiber-optic, and military applications. The rise in GaAs consumption is linked to 3G and 4G smartphones, which use up to 10 times more GaAs than older models. Gallium arsenide and gallium nitride are used in optoelectronic devices with a market share of $15.3 billion in 2015 and $18.5 billion in 2016. Aluminium gallium arsenide is used in high-power infrared laser diodes, while gallium nitride and indium gallium nitride are used in blue and violet optoelectronic devices, such as laser diodes and LEDs. For example, gallium nitride 405 nm diode lasers are used as violet light sources in higher-density Blu-ray Disc drives. Other major applications of gallium nitride include cable television, wireless infrastructure, power electronics, and satellites. The GaN radio frequency device market was estimated at $370 million in 2016 and $420 million in 2016. Multijunction photovoltaic cells for satellite power use molecular-beam or metalorganic vapour-phase epitaxy of gallium arsenide, indium gallium phosphide, or indium gallium arsenide; the Mars Exploration Rovers and several satellites use triple-junction gallium arsenide on germanium cells. Gallium is also a component in photovoltaic compounds like copper indium gallium selenium sulfide (Cu(In,Ga)(Se,S)2), used in solar panels as a cost-efficient alternative to crystalline silicon. Gallium readily alloys with most metals and is used in low-melting alloys. The nearly eutectic alloy of gallium, indium, and tin is a room-temperature liquid used in medical thermometers, known as Galinstan (with "-stan" referring to tin), having a melting point of −19 °C (−2.2 °F). This alloy is used to cool computer chips and as a thermal paste replacement in high-performance computing. Gallium alloys have been evaluated as substitutes for mercury dental amalgams but have not gained wide acceptance. Liquid gallium-indium alloys have been found to precipitate gaseous CO2 into solid carbon and are being researched for carbon capture and removal. Due to high surface tension and deformability, gallium-based liquid metals can be used to create actuators by controlling surface tension, with potential applications in artificial muscle for robotic actuation. Plutonium in nuclear weapon pits is stabilized in the δ phase and made machinable by alloying with gallium. Although gallium has no biological function, gallium ions behave like iron(III) in the body and are used in pharmaceuticals and radiopharmaceuticals. Interest in gallium's anticancer properties arose when 67Ga(III) citrate localized to tumor sites in animals. Clinical trials show gallium nitrate has antineoplastic activity against non-Hodgkin's lymphoma and urothelial cancers. New gallium-ligand complexes such as tris(8-quinolinolato)gallium(III) (KP46) and gallium maltolate are under development. Gallium nitrate (brand name Ganite) is used intravenously to treat hypercalcemia from bone tumor metastasis by interfering with osteoclast function. Gallium maltolate, an oral, highly absorbable gallium(III) ion, is anti-proliferative to cancer and some bacteria that take it instead of ferric iron (Fe3+), and is being tested for cancer, infectious, and inflammatory diseases. When gallium ions replace iron(III) in bacteria like Pseudomonas, they disrupt respiration because iron is redox-active while gallium is not. A complex amine-phenol Ga(III) compound MR045 is selectively toxic to chloroquine-resistant malaria parasites by inhibiting hemozoin crystallization. Gallium-67 salts such as gallium citrate and gallium nitrate are used as radiopharmaceuticals in gallium scans, where the radioactive isotope 67Ga is used and the gallium compound is unimportant. The body handles Ga3+ as if it were iron(III).

Ferric iron (Fe³⁺) is a key component in biological respiration, and researchers are investigating a compound containing gallium in clinical and preclinical trials for treating cancers, infectious diseases, and inflammatory conditions. When gallium ions substitute for iron(III) in bacteria like Pseudomonas, they disrupt respiration because iron is redox-active and facilitates electron transfer, whereas gallium is redox-inactive, leading to bacterial death. A complex amine-phenol Ga(III) compound, MR045, is selectively toxic to malaria parasites resistant to chloroquine, as both compounds inhibit the crystallization of hemozoin, a byproduct of blood digestion in parasites. Gallium-67 salts, such as gallium citrate and gallium nitrate, are used in nuclear medicine imaging (gallium scan) where the radioactive isotope ⁶⁷Ga is employed; the specific gallium compound is unimportant because Ga³⁺ behaves like Fe³⁺ in the body, concentrating in areas of inflammation or rapid cell division, enabling imaging of these sites. Gallium-68, a positron emitter with a half-life of 68 minutes, is used in PET-CT diagnostics when linked to pharmaceuticals like DOTATOC (for neuroendocrine tumors) and DOTA-TATE (for neuroendocrine metastasis and lung neuroendocrine cancers, including certain microcytomas); it is produced via chemical extraction from germanium-68 in gallium-68 generators. Gallium is used in neutrino detection, notably in the SAGE experiment at the Baksan Neutrino Observatory in Russia, which contains 55–57 tonnes of liquid gallium, and in the earlier GALLEX experiment in Italy, which used 12.2 tons of watered gallium-71; solar neutrinos caused a few ⁷¹Ga atoms to become radioactive ⁷¹Ge, detected in the experiment, revealing a 40% deficit in solar neutrino flux compared to theory—later explained by improved detectors and theories (e.g., SNO). Gallium serves as a liquid metal ion source in focused ion beams, such as in creating the world's smallest book, Teeny Ted from Turnip Town. It is also an additive in glide wax for skis and low-friction materials. Materials scientists consider gallium promising for flexible and wearable electronics. Gallium disrupts the protective oxide layer on aluminum, enabling water to react with aluminum in AlGa to produce hydrogen gas. A common chemist joke involves using gallium spoons to serve tea, as gallium resembles aluminum in appearance, and the spoons melt in hot tea. Advances in trace element analysis have detected dissolved gallium in the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans, with concentrations in the Beaufort Sea recently reported; typical dissolved gallium levels in the Pacific at depths <~150 m are 4–6 pmol/kg, while in the Atlantic at depths >~350 m, they are 25–28 pmol/kg. Gallium enters oceans primarily via aeolian input and is geochemically similar to aluminum, being less reactive; due to its similar dissolved profile and longer surface water residence time, gallium acts as a tracer for aluminum and for aeolian inputs of iron, particularly in the northwest Pacific, south and central Atlantic Oceans; for instance, low gallium surface waters in the subpolar northwest Pacific suggest low dust input, explaining high-nutrient, low-chlorophyll conditions. Metallic gallium is not toxic, but several gallium compounds are; gallium halide complexes are toxic, and the Ga³⁺ ion in soluble gallium salts forms an insoluble hydroxide when injected in large doses, causing nephrotoxicity in animals; at lower doses, soluble gallium is well-tolerated, does not accumulate, and is excreted mainly through urine in two phases: a first phase with a biological half-life of 1 hour and a second phase with a half-life of 25 hours. Inhaled Ga₂O₃ particles are likely toxic.
